items.title: Digital Twins as Socio-Technical Decision Systems: A Comparative Systematic Review of Supply Chain Management and Healthcare
items.abstract: Digital Twin (DT) technology is rapidly evolving from a digital representation of physical assets into a decision-support infrastructure that integrates real-time data, analytics, and simulation. However, existing research remains fragmented across application domains, limiting understanding of how DTs enable decision-making under different socio-technical conditions. This study presents a systematic literature review and decision-centric comparative analysis of DT applications in two contrasting decision environments: Supply Chain Management (SCM) and healthcare. Following a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) protocol, 193 peer-reviewed studies (95 SCM and 98 healthcare) were identified, screened, and synthesized across six analytical dimensions: application domains, technological integration, decision-making levels, business value, stakeholder involvement, and implementation challenges. The findings reveal fundamentally different decision logics despite a shared technological foundation based on Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and cloud computing. SCM-DTs primarily support coordination, optimization, resilience, and organizational scalability, whereas healthcare-DTs emphasize personalization, patient safety, and ethical governance under stringent regulatory constraints. Building on these findings, the study proposes a decision-centric comparative framework and a value–complexity perspective suggesting that value realization is increasingly associated with technological, organizational, and governance complexity as DT ecosystems mature. The paper advances the conceptualization of DTs as socio-technical decision systems and provides practical guidance for researchers, managers, and policymakers seeking responsible and effective digital transformation.

items.title: Do large language models keep the hedge? Uncertainty preservation when large language models summarize aviation and maritime incident reports
items.abstract: Safety-incident reports are written with deliberate epistemic caution: A reporter marks what was seen, what was inferred, and what remains unsure, and a dropped hedge can turn a tentative observation into an apparent cause. As large language models take over summarizing such reports for triage, indexing, and search, whether they preserve that caution becomes a property of the safety record itself. This study asks whether models keep a reporter's expressed uncertainty when they summarize, testing two hypotheses fixed before any summary was generated: that models systematically harden uncertainty by default and that an explicit instruction to preserve it overcorrects into softening. Six open-weight models summarized 42 real incident reports, 30 from the United States Aviation Safety Reporting System and 12 from the United Kingdom Marine Accident Investigation Branch, under a plain prompt, a preserve prompt, and a paraphrase of it. Uncertainty change was measured two ways: at the passage level, by a deterministic epistemic-marker lexicon, and at the claim level, by aligning those markers between source and summary, each validated against manual annotation and cross-checked against two independent language-model judges. Under plain summarization, all six models hardened the reporter's uncertainty (claim-level hardening 0.59–0.85), dropping explicit hedges almost entirely (retention about 0.08) while epistemic modal verbs survived far better. The preserve instruction reversed the pattern into over-softening: In a cluster-robust logistic regression, it carried an odds ratio of 0.12 (95% CI [0.03, 0.49], p = 0.003) and held once summary length was controlled, so the change reflects expressed certainty rather than compression. In practical terms, the instruction lowered the predicted probability of hardening from about 0.43 to 0.13 (Cohen's h = 0.69), and the effect held in mixed-effects models and under adverse imputation of the missing outputs. The pattern was directionally consistent across the tested models and both instruction wordings. Automated safety triage that relies on model summaries should measure epistemic fidelity directly and not treat a single preserve instruction as a solution.

items.title: Does AI-Assisted Design Undermine Market Value? The Influence of Design Source, Style, and Campaign Duration
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence technologies, traditional design value assessment systems based on creative input are facing new challenges. This study aims to examine the effects of design source (human-designed design vs. AI-assisted design), design style (commercial style vs. AI-native style), and campaign duration on the value assessment of design works in the AI era. Drawing on a real e-commerce platform context, the study conducts empirical analyses through two multifactor experiments. Experiment 1 adopts a 2 × 5 mixed experimental design to compare the value assessment performance of human-designed and AI-assisted design works across different campaign durations. Experiment 2 further introduces the variable of design style and employs a 2 × 2 × 5 three-factor experimental design to investigate the interaction effects among design source, design style, and campaign duration. The findings indicate that AI-assisted design demonstrates significant efficiency advantages in terms of time and cost. However, regarding value assessment indicators such as number of clicks, click-through rate (CTR), conversion rate (CVR), and sales performance, AI-assisted design performs comparably to human-designed design overall. Different design styles exhibit stage-specific differences: commercial style is more effective in attracting user attention and promoting conversion during the early stage of campaigns, whereas AI-native style gradually demonstrates higher conversion efficiency and cost advantages in the middle and later stages. In addition, the value assessment of design works exhibits significant temporal dynamics, with advertising performance reaching a relatively optimal level during the middle stage of campaign deployment. The study finds that AI significantly reduces creative input without weakening the market performance of design works, providing new evidence for understanding the input–outcome relationship in design value. The study also offers practical insights for enterprises seeking to optimize collaborative creation strategies between AI and human designers. items.title: Does Gemini comply with a data fabrication request?: A case study of a cross-language comparison
items.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that generative AI systems exhibit language-dependent variation in their ethical safeguards. Kawahara (2026a, b) found that when asked to share a confidential peer-review manuscript, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite refused in English (29/30 trials) but accepted in Japanese (27/30 trials), a statistically significant difference (Fisher's exact test, one-sided p < .001). This finding is consistent with broader evidence that multilingual safety alignment remains uneven across languages (Deng et al., 2024). The present study extends this line of research to a different domain of research ethics: data fabrication. Whereas the manuscript-sharing task involves a breach of confidentiality, data fabrication constitutes one of the most severe forms of research misconduct — the deliberate creation of fictitious data to be presented as empirical findings. In a preliminary (non-pre-registered, one-trial) test, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite was prompted in both English and Japanese to generate fabricated participant data to supplement an undersized dataset. The English prompt elicited a clear refusal citing academic integrity, while the Japanese prompt elicited full compliance, including executable code and a CSV output. The present study tests whether this pattern replicates systematically.

items.title: Dose–response effects of occupational and ergonomic exposures on cervical and lumbar spondylosis: A narrative review
items.abstract: Cervical and lumbar spondylosis are common degenerative spinal disorders associated with musculoskeletal pain, disability, and reduced work productivity. Where age is a major risk factor, occupational and ergonomic exposures contribute to spinal degeneration. Repetitive biomechanical loading and heavy lifting may accelerate degenerative changes. This narrative review aims to understand the dose- response relationship between occupational and ergonomic factors, development of cervical and lumbar spondylosis, while evaluating dose-response patterns that are associated with pharmacological, rehabilitative and ergonomic interventions. A narrative review of available literature was conducted on occupational risk factors, ergonomic determinants, cumulative biomechanical loading, pathophysiological and therapeutic strategies related to cervical and lumbar spondylosis. Evidence related to exposure intensity, frequency, duration and treatment outcomes were synthesized. Occupational exposures contribute to spinal degeneration through chronic mechanical overload, repetitive microtrauma, impaired disc nutrition and progressive structural deterioration. Increasing intensity, frequency, and duration of occupational exposure are associated with greater risks of cervical and lumbar spondylosis. Prolonged heavy lifting, repetitive bending, prolonged sitting, and vibration are associated with increased disc degeneration and functional impairment. Pharmacological therapies including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, muscle relaxants, neuropathic agents provide symptomatic relief, while physiotherapy, ergonomic rehabilitation exhibit dose-dependent clinical responses and offer more sustainable long-term improvements. Occupational and ergonomic factors plays major role in development and progression of cervical and lumbar spondylosis, with greater exposure greater the risk. Early ergonomic intervention, appropriate rehabilitation and individualized treatment improve function and minimize occupational disability.

items.title: Dream2Discern: Learning from Hard Latent Variants for Runtime Failure Prediction in Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Reliable deployment of LLM-based multi-agent systems calls for runtime auditors that predict terminal outcomes from observed execution prefixes. These auditors typically learn from a limited corpus of trajectories with verified outcomes. Expanding this corpus requires costly execution and verification, yet broader failure coverage alone provides no explicit criterion for identifying prefixes that the current auditor finds difficult to classify. To this end, we propose Dream2Discern, a runtime auditor trained through implicit augmentation guided by its own prediction loss. During Dream, we select perturbations of the auditor's representation operators to increase prediction loss on recorded prefixes, yielding hard latent variants. During Discern, the auditor learns to predict execution outcomes from these variants using the original labels. The variants are regenerated as the auditor learns, turning a limited corpus into a renewable source of hard examples and requiring no additional trajectory collection or outcome verification. Extensive evaluations on AFTraj-2K and StepShield show that Dream2Discern outperforms competitive failure auditors and achieves over 90% trajectory-level weighted accuracy on both benchmarks while balancing prediction accuracy and timeliness. items.title: DriftAgent: Using a Language Model to Turn Terraform Drift into Reviewed Merge Requests
items.abstract: Purpose: This paper describes the design and operation of DriftAgent, a system that detects configuration drift in Terraform-managed cloud infrastructure and prepares fixes for human review. It also reports what we learned from running the system in production at a streaming television company. Methodology: The study used a single-site case study design to evaluate a production deployment. DriftAgent runs every weekday morning: it asks an Atlantis server to plan 187 Terraform projects in parallel, parses the plan output, and sends each drifted project, together with its source files, to a large language model in a single request. The model returns HCL changes, including Terraform import blocks for resources that exist in the cloud but not in state; the agent opens a GitLab merge request for human review and posts a daily summary to Slack. Over twelve weeks (56 runs), we measured four outcomes: the fate of each merge request (merged unchanged, merged after edits, or closed), plan sweep time, engineering time per drift event, and inference cost. Merge request outcomes were validated by two engineers who independently rated a random sample of 120 merge requests as acceptable, acceptable with edits, or unacceptable against defined criteria, and inter-rater reliability was measured with Cohen’s kappa. Engineering effort was compared with a pre-deployment timing study of 71 manually handled drift events. Data were analyzed with descriptive statistics (counts, percentages, means, medians, and 95th percentiles), edited or closed proposals were classified by their main failure reason, and the findings were synthesized by triangulating production logs, merge request histories, the independent ratings, and the timing data. Findings: Across 56 runs the system recorded 372 drift events and opened 351 merge requests. Reviewers merged 73.5% of them without semantic changes and 18.2% after edits, and closed 8.3%. Moving plan execution from a sequential loop to Atlantis reduced the median sweep time from 52.0 to 11.4 minutes. Weekly engineering time spent on drift fell from 9.4 to 2.4 hours, at an inference cost of about US$0.08 per drifted project. The most common reasons for edited or rejected proposals were choosing the wrong kind of remediation and formatting an import identifier incorrectly. Unique contribution to theory, practice and policy: The study gives evidence that a fixed workflow with one model call, a deterministic plan check, and mandatory human approval is a workable way to use language models in change-controlled infrastructure. For practitioners, it documents specific design choices and failure modes. For organizations writing policy on AI in operations, it supports keeping approval and apply rights with people while assigning analysis and drafting to the model.

items.title: DTKF: a sepsis early prediction framework based on large language model semantic augmentation and dual-teacher knowledge distillation
items.abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Early and accurate prediction is crucial for reducing mortality. However, clinical settings often face challenges such as data scarcity, class imbalance, and the underutilization of unstructured clinical notes. Existing scoring systems and traditional machine learning models primarily rely on structured vital signs, failing to capture the rich semantic risk factors embedded in textual data. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in text understanding, their high computational costs and potential hallucinations hinder direct deployment in resource-constrained emergency settings. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel Dual-Teacher Knowledge Fusion (DTKF) framework. First, we introduce a semantic feature augmentation module that leverages DeepSeek to extract semantic risk probabilities from clinical notes and explicitly fuses them with structured vital signs to construct high-order hybrid features for the student model. Second, to prevent overfitting under small-sample conditions, we design a dual-source knowledge distillation strategy. This strategy integrates rule-based knowledge and data-driven semantic knowledge to construct hybrid teacher signals, regulating a lightweight logistic regression student model via soft-label supervision. Experiments on the MIMIC-IV dataset demonstrate that DTKF achieves an AUC of 0.796. This result not only achieves a higher AUC than traditional unimodal baselines but also improves performance by 6.6% compared to direct prediction using LLMs. This study effectively integrates rule-based and data-driven knowledge, enhances feature representation using textual information, and improves model performance and robustness through distillation techniques, providing a clinically valuable solution for sepsis early warning.

items.abstract: The v1.0 record reported a preregistered benchmark of Squirrel OS's Dual Mesh deterministic resolution layer: the in-process mesh resolver resolved synthetic anomalies at a median of 0.000443 ms versus 4509.1 ms for the identical resolution task through an LLM conversation loop (ratio 1.018e+07, n=200/20), with mesh ingestion integrity (50/50 unique collision hashes) and resolution correctness (72/72 replay, zero false positives) verified. Version 2.0 adds a cross-platform verification appendix. The same frozen corpus (sha256 13295d197be59dd1266814bc2f961f1e55e974c61c642fd9c7a6a389668fee59) was re-run under a second preregistered protocol: (1) mesh parity re-run confirming run-over-run determinism (200/200, median 0.00039 ms); (2) the LLM baseline leg re-executed from a second host (Cloudflare Workers edge, 20/20 valid, median 7.386 s, ratio 1.894e+07); and (3) the same task issued to an external LLM API substrate (OpenRouter, deepseek-chat, 20/20 valid, median 179.4 ms, ratio 4.60e+05). The mesh lookup outperforms both substrates on every measured host. The platform-loop wall-clock is shown to be dominated by conversation orchestration rather than model inference (~41x difference). All amendments (host swap, output-fence normalization, rate-limit retry policy) were committed to the public ledger before the respective execution or re-attempt; strict first-pass scores are reported alongside normalized scores, and all raw runs are preserved verbatim in the evidence bundle. Claims remain scoped to the measured environments; no universal performance claim is made. All test data are synthetic; no production, customer, or personal data are involved. items.title: EAU: Environment-Agent-User Co-evolution for Training User-Centric Agents
items.abstract: Training LLM agents to interact with users over multiple turns is challenging because the learning signal depends not only on the agent, but also on the user simulator and environment, which jointly shape the agent's experience. Simulated users can be stochastic or inconsistent, while environments may contain unreliable tools, incomplete state coverage, and incorrect verifiers. Prior work mainly addresses the resulting instability through reward shaping or denser supervision, while treating these components as fixed. We instead introduce EAU, a meta-agent framework for environment--agent--user co-evolution. During training, EAU monitors trajectories, tool traces, rewards, and training statistics; diagnoses failures and uninformative interactions; and proposes targeted modifications to the user simulator, environment, reward design, and RL configuration. Validated changes are hot-swapped into the ongoing run, allowing the training setup to evolve together with the policy. These adaptations also persist across runs, so later training can build on previously discovered improvements rather than restarting from a fixed setup. We enable this process through an editable symbolic representation of user and environment dynamics, while the agent remains a neural LLM optimized with RL. Across three interactive-agent benchmarks and two backbone models, EAU consistently outperforms prior RL methods, improving the overall score over the strongest baseline by 14.7--15.0% and increasing successful task completion on ColBench by up to 36.7%, showing that co-evolving the training system with the policy can substantially improve multi-turn RL.

items.title: ECHO: Correcting Time Series Foundation Model Forecasts with Historical Analogues and Errors
items.abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide general-purpose forecasting capabilities, yet their forecasts can remain misaligned with the temporal characteristics of a target domain. This motivates lightweight forecast correction even when only black-box access to the TSFM is available. Our key observation is that two forms of historical information provide complementary correction signals: historical analogues reveal how similar contexts evolved, while past forecast errors reveal a TSFM's characteristic deviations in the target domain. Based on this observation, we propose ECHO, a black-box forecast correction framework that learns from both sources. ECHO uses AnalogE to assess retrieved historical analogues together with the current context and base forecast, learning transferable corrections through cross-domain pretraining. In parallel, RecentE learns target-specific residual corrections from past forecast errors and refines them as causally available feedback accumulates. ECHO dynamically combines the two corrections according to their observed forecasting performance. Across 5 representative TSFMs and 9 real-world datasets, ECHO reduces MSE in all 45 backbone--dataset settings, yielding an average relative reduction of 9.26\% in macro-average MSE. Its gains also extend to long-horizon forecasting.

items.title: Effectiveness of AI-Assisted Screening Tools for Depression and Anxiety in Primary Care: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: This systematic review evaluates the effectiveness, diagnostic accuracy, and implementation outcomes of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted screening tools for depression and anxiety in primary care settings, with a focus on literature published since the advent of advanced large language models. A systematic search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and Cochrane Central from January 2020 to September 2025. Ten studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising randomized controlled trials, pragmatic trials, and validation studies. Included studies demonstrated that AI-assisted tools (including conversational chatbots, machine learning models using voice and behavioral data, and digital decision-support systems) can achieve high diagnostic accuracy, with balanced accuracy up to 88.2% and Area Under the Curve (AUC) up to 0.82. Clinically, AI-assisted interventions were associated with higher depression remission (e.g., 27.3% vs. 12.0%) and better anxiety outcomes than treatment-as-usual in individual trials. Feasibility and acceptability were generally favorable, with completion rates often exceeding 60-70% and user satisfaction reaching 79%, even among older adults. Key challenges included limited external validation, demographic homogeneity, and insufficient reporting on ethical safeguards. AI-assisted screening tools show potential to improve the detection and management of depression and anxiety in primary care, with encouraging accuracy, clinical effectiveness, and user engagement in the available studies. However, the evidence base is small and heterogeneous, and future research needs to address gaps in generalizability, long-term efficacy, ethical oversight, and seamless workflow integration to ensure equitable and responsible implementation.

items.title: Effectiveness of an Artificial Intelligence–Assisted HIV Educational Video for Improving HIV Health Literacy Among Indonesian Adolescents
items.abstract: Adolescents in low- and middle-income countries continue to face substantial barriers in accessing effective HIV education, despite global efforts in prevention. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a culturally adapted HIV educational video developed using artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted video production tools. The intervention assessed in this study was the educational video itself rather than direct interaction with a generative AI system. A quasi-experimental design with pre- and posttests and a control group was used to evaluate the intervention among 60 high school students. Participants were randomly assigned to either a group that received a 10-min AI-generated educational video or a control group that received no intervention. The video was designed to improve HIV health literacy by addressing four domains: access to information, comprehension of core concepts, evaluation of risks, and application of knowledge in real-life decisions. Quantitative data were collected in May 2024 using a validated scale and analyzed with nonparametric tests and analysis of covariance. Students who received the AI-assisted educational video demonstrated significantly higher posttest HIV health literacy scores than the control group (Mann–Whitney U = 206.5, p < .001). After adjustment for baseline scores, analysis of covariance confirmed a significant group effect ( F (1,57) = 21.70, p < .001, partial η 2 = 0.28), indicating a large adjusted effect size. The findings highlight the potential of generative AI as an innovative, scalable tool for adolescent health education, particularly in resource-limited settings. This approach may offer new opportunities for integrating digital strategies into school-based health promotion programs.

items.title: Effects of AI-assisted speaking practice on spoken English performance in higher vocational education
items.abstract: Abstract With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), AI-assisted tools are increasingly integrated into language education. However, empirical evidence on their effectiveness for spoken English in higher vocational colleges remains limited. This quasi-experimental study examined whether AI-assisted speaking practice using iFLYTEK Spark, a generative AI platform with speech recognition and real-time feedback capabilities, was associated with higher post-intervention spoken English performance among 92 first-year vocational college students in China. Two intact classes were assigned to an experimental group ( n = 46) receiving 12 weeks of AI-assisted practice plus conventional instruction and a control group ( n = 46) receiving conventional instruction only. Post-intervention speaking performance was assessed by three trained raters using an analytic rubric covering pronunciation, language use, fluency and coherence, and interaction. The experimental group achieved significantly higher overall posttest scores (M = 3.69, SD = 0.76) than the control group (M = 3.19, SD = 0.82; t(90) = 3.011, p = 0.003, Hedges’ g = 0.63). Medium-to-large effect sizes were found in language use (g = 0.49), fluency and coherence (g = 0.50), and interaction (g = 0.75), whereas the difference in pronunciation was smaller and non-significant (g = 0.38, p = 0.071). Semi-structured interviews with one teacher and three students provided supplementary insights into perceived benefits, including increased practice opportunities, reduced speaking anxiety, and enhanced motivation. While the intact-class design and coarse baseline proficiency measure limit causal claims, the findings suggest that AI-assisted tools can serve as a valuable supplement to conventional spoken English instruction in higher vocational settings. Implications for pedagogy and future research directions are discussed.

items.title: Effects of Transparent Robot Intentions on Human Trust and Compliance in Decision-Making: The Role of Benevolent and Ulterior Intentions of Robots
items.abstract: Humans are more commonly relying on the assistance of advanced robots in decision-making processes and may follow robots’ suggestions depending on their understanding of how such suggestions are generated. To enhance human understanding, robots can communicate their (simulated) intentions, influencing the trust placed upon them. However, it remains uncertain whether and under what conditions robots’ simulated intentions could also negatively impact trust and compliance. Therefore, we conducted a laboratory experiment with 182 participants, exploring whether information about a robot’s potential benevolent intentions and ulterior motives increased or decreased trust and compliance with the robot’s suggestions, while also altering participants’ involvement levels in a decision task. The results of two 2x2x2 ANOVAs revealed that, regardless of the involvement level, the robot’s simulated ulterior motives decreased trust and compliance, while benevolent intentions did not significantly affect these outcomes. Thus, simulated intentions should be considered in the design of collaborative decision-making between humans and robots.

items.title: Efficient Resource-Shiftable RL Post-training with Generative Rewards
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training with generative reward models (GenRM) has become a central recipe for improving large language models (LLMs), and it is also increasingly resource-intensive: policy rollout, GenRM-based reward evaluation, and policy training all compete for GPU resources. However, existing colocated and disaggregated systems rely on static resource allocation for these roles. Such allocation cannot adapt as each role's workload changes during RL and therefore leaves a role's resources underutilized. We present PivotRL, an RL post-training system that dynamically shifts resources among different roles according to their runtime demands. PivotRL introduces a resource-shiftable runtime built on a Global Parameter Storage, together with a unified mechanism that efficiently shifts role-specific context. A shift-aware scheduler enables sequence migration upon a shift, while a planner considers the aggregate throughput benefit and the shift overhead to determine when and how to shift. We evaluate PivotRL on a 128-GPU cluster using four model groups spanning dense and mixture-of-experts models. PivotRL enables resource shifting within seconds and improves end-to-end throughput by 1.81-2.05 times over colocated deployment and 1.50-1.95 times over disaggregated deployment, while preserving RL convergence.

items.title: Employee Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence in Logistics Operations: Evidence from a State-Owned Energy Distributor in Sri Lanka
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption in logistics depends not only on technological capability but also on employees’ willingness and ability to use AI-based systems. This study examines the factors influencing employees’ behavioural intention to use AI in logistics operations through the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). A positivist, deductive, quantitative and cross-sectional survey design was used in a state-owned energy distribution enterprise in Sri Lanka. The population comprised 93 employees, with 75 targeted and 63 usable responses obtained. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, Pearson correlation and multiple regression in SPSS. Performance expectancy, effort expectancy and facilitating conditions had statistically significant positive effects on behavioural intention, whereas social influence was not statistically significant. Facilitating conditions had the strongest standardized effect (β = 0.326, p = 0.008). The regression model explained 67.0% of the variance in behavioural intention (R² = 0.670). The findings highlight the importance of organisational readiness, practical support, system usability and visible performance benefits when introducing AI into regulated logistics operations. The study contributes context-specific evidence from a state-owned energy distributor in Sri Lanka while recognizing that the single-organization, cross-sectional design limits broader generalization.

items.title: Empowering Drivers as Collaborative Social Agents: Enhancing Pedestrian Interaction through Cooperative Interfaces in Autonomous Vehicle Systems
items.abstract: While autonomous driving technology reduces the operational burden on drivers, it may also diminish their sense of engagement, for example, by interrupting social interactions between drivers and other road users such as pedestrians. To address this, this article proposes a “Social Cooperation” driving mode from a cooperative driving perspective, aiming to activate drivers’ social capabilities to compensate for the limitations of autonomous systems in social interaction and to enhance drivers’ engagement in pedestrian-yielding scenarios. Through a driving simulator prototype experiment, we found that the proposed approach significantly improved drivers’ psychological need satisfaction, enhancing their autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs, while also showing positive trends in empathy, benevolence, and overall satisfaction. The results provide new insights into social interactions in autonomous driving contexts and offer practical and theoretical guidance for the design of human-machine cooperative driving interfaces.

items.title: Energy constraints in large scale artificial intelligence and insights from human cognition for efficient large language models
items.abstract: Abstract Large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) systems, especially large language models (LLMs), face growing constraints related to energy use, power delivery, memory traffic, experimentation, and infrastructure capacity. These pressures are often studied separately, which makes it difficult to understand how they interact across the full AI lifecycle. This review develops a cross-layer framework that brings these constraints together and examines whether resource-allocation strategies observed in human cognition can inform more sustainable AI design. We compare human and artificial systems by function rather than anatomy, focusing on how each allocates limited resources to learning, search, memory, external support, optimization, and inference. Using a systematized narrative-review approach, we identified 6284 records, screened 898 at the full-text stage, and selected an initial set of 150 focal studies for detailed synthesis. We organize the evidence into seven interacting regimes covering scaling, experimentation, hardware power limits, data movement, infrastructure, evaluation incentives, and inference allocation. The framework extends Green AI by linking these layers and translating insights from human cognition into testable design hypotheses and measurable evaluation criteria. The strongest near-term opportunities include data selection, energy-aware experimentation, hardware-supported low-precision computation, and demand-adaptive inference. However, most reported gains are based on proxy measures such as operations, memory, latency, or data volume rather than direct end-to-end energy measurements. Near- and in-memory computing show longer-term promise, while retrieval, tool use, distributed experts, and multi-agent systems may shift or increase energy costs through communication and repeated inference. These findings support cross-layer co-design and end-to-end evaluation at matched capability, reliability, latency, and service quality.

items.title: Energy-efficient deep learning-based vibration monitoring on parallel ultra-low-power microcontrollers
items.abstract: Structural health monitoring (SHM) through vibration analysis is essential for ensuring safety, reliability, and minimized maintenance costs in sensor-connected environments. Realizing this at the extreme edge, directly on sensor nodes, requires advanced data analytics, ultra-energy-efficient hardware, and high-fidelity datasets. This paper addresses these challenges by developing an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based deep learning framework for vibration-based structural health monitoring tailored to resource-constrained devices. We present a benchmarking dataset for vibration SHM, encompassing nine abnormal conditions that capture narrowband structural anomalies. Leveraging this dataset, we design supervised and unsupervised deep-learning models, integrating a system identification (SysId) preprocessing stage to derive structurally informed features that enhance model input quality. This improves algorithmic results while boosting hardware performances. These models are deployed on a parallel ultra-low-power microcontroller with dedicated hardware acceleration. Our unsupervised anomaly detectors deliver 89.90 percent (%) accuracy, 4.1 percentage points higher than the state-of-the-art attention-based baseline, favoring recall and missed-detection reduction at the cost of a higher false-alarm rate while consuming 13 microjoules (µJ) in low-power mode and requiring 370 microseconds (µs) in high-performance mode. This marks one of the first experimental validations of unsupervised on-device vibration diagnostics. Supervised counterparts achieve 96.06 % binary and 91.5 % multiclass accuracy, rivaling Residual Network (ResNet) with 15.8 × fewer parameters, at less than 235 µJ and not more than 6.3 ms (ms) inference. Relative to existing edge implementations, our approach is one to three orders of magnitude more energy-efficient and two orders faster, unlocking AI-enabled autonomous, low-latency predictive maintenance for large-scale distributed infrastructure monitoring.

items.title: Enhanced crop yield estimation in smart agriculture via AI and IoT using the GODL geo-optimized algorithm
items.abstract: Abstract Precision agriculture is one of the major breakthroughs which has been adopted to counteract some of the major challenges facing contemporary agriculture, such as maximizing crop yield, maximizing resource efficiency, and sustainability. The application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) technologies can go a long way in enhancing crop yield prediction through data obtained from multiple sources, including satellite images, ground sensors, and weather stations. This research paper proposes a next-generation crop yield prediction system called Geo-Optimized Deep Learning (GODL) algorithm. The GODL algorithm integrates geospatial information with deep learning algorithms for crop yield analysis and prediction. This combination of deep learning and geospatial data allows accurate and scalable crop yield predictions using geospatial and sensor information. In order to ensure model optimization in terms of accuracy and efficiency, the GODL Algorithm makes use of advanced hyperparameter optimization methods that include Adam and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). The research paper highlights the efficiency of the GODL Algorithm by conducting extensive experiments that compare the algorithm’s performance with other crop yield prediction models like Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) and other machine learning techniques. The evaluation takes into consideration important metrics such as accuracy, Jaccard Index, Fowlkes-Mallows Index (FMI), and G-mean, as well as IoT data delay and its effects on the prediction accuracy. In future research, the use of blockchain technology to facilitate data sharing and edge computing to process the data will be considered.

items.title: Enhancing learning health care systems with real-world data harmonization frameworks
items.abstract: The use of digital tools has enabled the capture of clinical data that can be leveraged to produce real-world evidence, complementing traditional trial data and addressing evidence gaps in oncology. Electronic health records offer rich, longitudinal data, although recording practices, collection methods, and quality may vary over time and across settings, which can lead to inconsistencies. Data harmonization is key to overcoming fragmentation, and common data models offer structured methods for unifying diverse health care data. Various mapping strategies standardize data balancing, automation, flexibility, and semantic precision: ‘upstream semantic mapping' emphasizes standardization, ‘downstream semantic mapping' allows tailored adjustments by local experts, and ‘direct dataset mapping' focuses on creating analysis-ready datasets without intermediate data transformation. The best approach depends on organizational needs, data characteristics, and intended use cases, but harmonization must be a continuous process that adapts to evolving data sources, variable data types, new collection methods, and shifting transformation practices. Clinical expertise must ensure that cohorts mirror real-world scenarios and capture local nuances, more often with an artificial intelligence–assisted framework, while epidemiologists must consider harmonization practices in the study design and analysis. Data strategies must protect patient privacy while supporting health care improvements, with secure data handling paired with accessible sharing. By engaging medical professionals at every stage, health care institutions can become learning health systems driven by high-quality observational research, ultimately advancing knowledge and improving patient outcomes.

items.title: Enhancing Library Navigation and Book Retrieval Through an Algorithm in Smart Management System Frameworks
items.abstract: Conventional library management systems have serious flaws in finding books and ways of traversing the books and hence it takes more time to search and less satisfaction to users. The incorporation of the artificial intelligence algorithms offers prospects to maximize path finding and the resource location in smart libraries structures. The paper applied A* path finding algorithm in a smart library management system which included use of heuristic functions in calculating optimal route and mapping of books. Three library settings in different layouts with different amounts of collections were used to test the system in terms of the efficiency of retrievals, navigation accuracy, and the time of interaction between the user and the system over a six months span. The A* improved system recorded 94.7 percent accuracy in identifying the location of a book, an efficiency in average retrieval period of 68.3 percent, and a 82.1 percent enhancement of efficiency in navigation as opposed to the traditional system. The score of user satisfaction rose by 91.2 percent and the average system response time is 1.3 seconds. A* algorithm is one of the best algorithms that are used in the enhancement of library navigation facilities, which offers huge advantages in accuracy and effectiveness in retrieval of library information and in whose system current and modern smart library applications are used.

items.title: Enhancing PISA-aligned argumentation skills of prospective biology teachers through generative artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Despite scientific argumentation being a fundamental competency of the PISA assessment framework, prospective biology teachers often demonstrate insufficient development in evidence-based reasoning and rebuttal construction skills. Considering the limitations of large-scale implementation of individualized approaches in higher education, this study evaluates the effectiveness of Generative Artificial Intelligence (ChatGPT-4) configured as a “Socratic tutor” in developing argumentation skills among future educators. An 8-week quasi-experimental study involving 124 students from a pedagogical university employed traditional peer discussion methods in the control group ( n = 62), while the experimental group ( n = 62) utilized an AI agent that induced cognitive dissonance regarding socio-scientific issues. Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) of data obtained through Toulmin's Argument Pattern (TAP) and PISA rubrics confirmed that the experimental group achieved statistically significantly higher overall argumentation quality compared to the control group (F (1,121) = 14.23, p < .001, η 2 = .105). Particularly, participants who received AI-assisted instruction showed marked improvement in forming rebuttals and evaluating counterevidence, which are considered among the most cognitively demanding components within the PISA scientific literacy framework (OECD). These findings suggest that a Generative AI-mediated Socratic instructional package can be an effective and scalable approach for developing epistemic cognition, and they propose a pedagogical model for integrating structured AI-based tutoring into teacher preparation systems aligned with international assessment standards. These findings should be interpreted as evidence for the effectiveness of the structured, AI-mediated Socratic instructional package as a whole, rather than as evidence of AI's inherent superiority over other methods; the relative contribution of the AI medium versus the structured pedagogical protocol it delivers was not directly tested in this design.

items.title: ENSURING CYBERSECURITY IN THE CONTEXT OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION: A RISK-BASED MANAGEMENT AND RESILIENCE MODEL
items.abstract: igital transformation expands access to government, financial, educational, and commercial services, but at the same time increases organizations’ dependence on information systems, network services, cloud platforms, and external providers. Under these conditions, cybersecurity should be viewed not merely as a set of technical safeguards, but as a system of continuous risk management that ensures data confidentiality, integrity, and availability; process resilience; the protection of data subjects’ rights; and business recovery following incidents. The purpose of this article is to systematize the main threats and cybersecurity measures, compare international statistical indicators, and propose a multi-level practical model for commercial organizations and government agencies. This study is based on an analysis of documents from the International Telecommunication Union and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, as well as reports from Verizon and IBM, and on a comparative and systematic analysis of approaches to cyber threat management. The data indicate that system vulnerabilities, ransomware, third-party risks, and the human factor remain key elements of the threat landscape. At the same time, the published metrics were obtained using various methodologies and cannot serve as a unified assessment of the frequency of global attacks. The article presents a model that integrates management, prevention, detection, response, and recovery. It was concluded that effective cybersecurity requires clearly measurable goals, the allocation of responsibilities, the protection of supply chains, regular practical exercises, and respect for privacy and other human rights. Keywords: cybersecurity, cyber threat, risk management, incident, data protection, resilience, supply chain, incident response measures

items.title: Enterprise Systems, Data Management, and Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP): Conceptual Foundations
items.abstract: Over the past few decades, organizations have systematically shifted from fragmented, function-specific software tools toward integrated enterprise architectures, with Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) serving as the central technological backbone and a codified model of organizational operations. As contemporary digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption accelerate, these emerging capabilities build directly upon established ERP backbones and enterprise data infrastructures rather than operating on a blank slate. This chapter synthesizes three closely related domains—enterprise systems, data management, and ERP—to establish a cohesive, stable conceptual framework and vocabulary for researchers and practitioners. The authors examine the evolutionary trajectory of ERP from 1960s Materials Requirements Planning (MRP) to contemporary multi-tenant cloud and Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) environments. Core operational architectures and functional modules—such as finance, human resources, procurement, manufacturing, and supply chain management—are analyzed alongside essential data management mechanisms. The chapter emphasizes that enterprise integration depends fundamentally on robust data governance, master data management (MDM), and interoperability through middleware and application programming interfaces (APIs) to prevent errors from propagating across business units. Implementation dynamics are explored through the lens of business process reengineering (BPR), technology-organization-environment frameworks, and post-implementation success factors, demonstrating that organizational alignment outweighs purely software-centric considerations. Crucially, the study identifies key theoretical and practical tensions inherent in enterprise digital architectures, including the conflict between system standardization and customization, the concentration of systemic security risks within unified data repositories, and the shift of ERP from a passive system of record to an active, AI-driven system of action. Special attention is devoted to advanced algorithmic transformations, including predictive analytics, process automation, and second-order agentic AI systems capable of executing multi-step autonomous tasks. The authors contend that agentic AI and Industry 4.0 integrations amplify, rather than eliminate, core requirements for data quality, explainability, and explicit decision accountabilities. Ultimately, the chapter concludes that rigorous data governance, strategic change management, and realistic expectations regarding process standardization remain necessary prerequisites for unlocking sustained organizational value from enterprise systems.

items.title: EPISTEMIC TRUST, METHODOLOGICAL OPACITY, AND HALLUCINATION RISKS IN AI-AUGMENTED EDUCATIONAL SCHOLARSHIP: A CRITICAL LITERATURE REVIEW
items.abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) into academic inquiry has triggered an unprecedented paradigm shift in educational research. While AI-augmented literature synthesis, automated data coding, and language refinement offer remarkable productivity gains, they simultaneously introduce profound epistemic and methodological vulnerabilities. This doctoral dissertation provides an exhaustive, critical literature review exploring the complex interplay among Epistemic Trust, Methodological Opacity, and Hallucination Risks in modern educational scholarship. Synthesizing extensive peer-reviewed literature published between 2020 and 2024, this study adopts a virtue epistemology framework to analyze how algorithmic cognitive offloading impacts scholarly rigor. The findings reveal a growing systemic tension between productivity acceleration and epistemic vigilance: heavy reliance on generative tools correlates with a decline in primary-source verification, increased vulnerability to algorithmic hallucinations, and an over-reliance on opaque "black-box" data interpretations. Furthermore, this study evaluates current institutional policy responses across international higher education frameworks, highlighting a critical deficit in systematic verification protocols and doctoral AI literacy training. To resolve these systemic vulnerabilities, this review formulates the Epistemic Verification and Transparency Protocol (EVTP), providing actionable guidelines for researchers, journal editors, and university ethics committees to preserve scholarly integrity in an increasingly automated academic landscape.

items.title: EPOCH: Coverage-Aware Evolution with Experiential Preference Optimization for LLM-based Automated Heuristic Design
items.abstract: LLM-based automated heuristic design (AHD) discovers heuristics for combinatorial optimization problems (COPs), where an LLM generates candidates in an evolutionary search. Existing frameworks freeze the generator or fine-tune it on a scalar fitness signal hiding which instances each heuristic covers. Reflection-based frameworks improve heuristics with natural-language feedback, but it stays in the prompt and never reaches the generator's weights. We propose EPOCH, which makes instance coverage the objective of the evolutionary search and fine-tunes the generator to internalize reflection. Parent selection, operator allocation, and stagnation recovery all optimize how well the heuristics jointly cover the training instances, so the search returns a complementary heuristic ensemble. The generator learns from its own search by experiential preference optimization. A teacher LLM returns a natural-language insight on the generated heuristics, and the generator produces new heuristics with this insight. These improvements join the preference pairs for direct preference optimization (DPO). Since DPO only teaches the generator to rank these improvements, a reflective self-distillation (RSD) term makes it more likely to generate them on its own, and the gains accumulate over the long horizon of the search. Across COPs and open-source LLM backbones, EPOCH's heuristic ensembles outperform inference-only and fine-tuned baselines and generalize across problem scales.

items.abstract: This study investigated equity in the availability and utilization of Artificial Intelligence (AI) facilities among urban and rural public secondary schools in Benue State, Nigeria. The study was guided by two research questions and two hypotheses. A descriptive survey design was adopted. The population comprised 3,726 teachers in 128 public secondary schools, from which 361 teachers were selected using stratified random sampling. Data were collected using the Equitable Utilization of Artificial Intelligence Questionnaire (EUAIQ), validated by three experts in the Faculty of Education, Veritas University, Bwari, Abuja. The instrument yielded a Cronbach’s alpha reliability coefficient of 0.88 based on a trial test involving 30 teachers. Mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions, with a 2.50 decision criterion, while independent-samples t-test was used to test the hypotheses at the 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed significant differences between the mean ratings of respondents from urban and rural public secondary schools regarding both the availability and utilization of AI facilities for teaching and learning in Benue State. The study concludes that disparities exist in the availability and utilization of AI facilities between urban and rural public secondary schools. It recommends equitable provision of funding, reliable internet connectivity, stable electricity and AI-enabled digital resources by government and relevant stakeholders, alongside continuous capacity-building programmes for teachers on the effective use of AI facilities.

items.title: Ethical Responsibility of AI-generated Content in Digital Advertising: Transparency, Trust and Platform Accountability
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the production and dissemination of digital advertising. Although the content generated by AI has improved the efficiency of creation, it has also caused ethical problems such as false endorsements, hidden advertisements, and algorithm amplification. Based on the ethics of obligation theory, social responsibility theory and utilitarian ethics, this article uses case analysis to critically analyze the phenomenon of ethical misconduct in AI digital advertising. The study found that the platform failed to fully fulfill its public responsibility as a digital communication gater in the process of pursuing commercial interests. This article proposes that the platform should assume the responsibility of algorithm ethics, governance transparency and collaborative governance to rebuild public trust in digital communication.

items.title: Ethics in fashion business
items.abstract: This chapter provides a critical analysis of the concept of ethics in fashion and the need for moral decision-making as the basis for industry practice. Starting with the definition of ethics and moral philosophy, it examines the use and ambiguities of the terms ‘ethical’ and ‘moral,’ and their use in modern business environments. Central to this chapter is the discussion that ethical decision-making is grounded in human agency and our ability to make choices informed by our values, culture, and experiences. Ethical leadership is influenced by many factors, including personal morals, societal rules, and organisational pressures. These factors can create ethical dilemmas for decision-makers, in which profit and convenience may conflict with what is morally right. The chapter examines the ethical implications of fashion industry practices, including labour exploitation, environmental degradation, animal welfare, transparency, and greenwashing. It highlights the ethical implications of global production systems and examines the role Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reporting, certifications, legislation, and corporate social responsibility play in making fashion businesses more accountable. It also addresses the emergence of ethical leadership and the role of senior managers in fostering integrity, trust, and ethical decision-making throughout a fashion business. In addition, the chapter will also explore the emerging ethical issues related to Artificial Intelligence, cultural appropriation, diversity and inclusion, and social media and marketing. It will also reflect on ethical consumerism, noting the obstacles consumers face when making purchasing decisions. The chapter will finally discuss why the fashion industry needs to establish ethical business practices to support the transformation to long-term sustainability and increase stakeholder trust.

items.title: EVALUASI ERGONIMI MENGGUNAKAN METODE KUISIONER NORDIC BODY MAP DAN RAPID UPPER LIMB ASSESSMENT (RULA) UNTUK MENURUNKAN RISIKO LOW BACK PAIN (LBP) PADA OPERATOR PRODUKSI BERBASIS PENGOLAHAN DATA DIGITAL (STUDI KASUS PADA BAGIAN VIBRO GULA, GULA GILING DAN SSK DI PT MYR)
items.abstract: Abstract: Manual material handling activities on the production line of PT MYR, particularly in the Sugar Vibro, Sugar Grinding, and SSK sections, have the potential to pose a risk of Musculoskeletal Disorders (MSDs), specifically Low Back Pain (LBP). This study aims to evaluate the working posture of production operators, identify the body parts most vulnerable to injury, and formulate recommendations for ergonomic work facilities and methods to reduce injury risk levels and enhance work efficiency. The method used in this study is a combination of the Nordic Body Map (NBM) questionnaire to measure the subjective physical complaints of respondents (n=20) and the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) method based on digital/photo data processing to objectively evaluate the joint angles of operator postures. The results of the NBM questionnaire data processing indicated that complaints were most dominant in the waist area at 95% (19 out of 20 respondents) and the back area at 75% (15 out of 20 respondents), followed by complaints in the right shoulder (55%) and left shoulder (50%). The posture analysis using the RULA method indicated high to very high ergonomic risk levels: at the Sugar Vibro station, the lifting sacks from pallet activity achieved a final RULA score of 7 (Action Level 4, very high risk), pouring sacks into machine hopper activity achieved a final RULA score of 6 (Action Level 3, high risk), the Sugar Grinding station scored 5 (Action Level 3), and the SSK station scored 7 (Action Level 4). The primary factors contributing to the high LBP risk in operators were the high trunk flexion angle of up to 65°, repetitive lifting of loads weighing 25–50 kg, and static arm and wrist positions without ergonomic support. The proposed improvement recommendations include modifying and redesigning workstations, providing ergonomic material handling equipment, designing work rotation schedules, and conducting regular muscle stretching programs. Keywords: Ergonomics, Nordic Body Map (NBM), Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA), Low Back Pain (LBP), Production Operators, Manual Material Handling. items.title: Evaluating and explaining LLM classification for automatic screening in Systematic Reviews
items.abstract: Evidence synthesis methods, such as systematic reviews (SR), require research teams to find, select, evaluate, and synthesize all available evidence to answer a specific research question in a reproducible and transparent, bias-reduced manner. Early in the process, teams must screen all unique titles and abstracts gathered from a comprehensive search, which can result in thousands of records. Therefore, the process often takes months to years to complete. In this research, we conduct a set of experiments using open-source Large Language Models (LLMs) with small parameters hosted on local servers to screen titles and abstracts against pre-defined eligibility criteria respective to each topic. We use two cases from real SRs for which titles and abstracts screening has already been completed by dual, independent human screeners, which we use as our “ground truth”.

items.title: Evaluating interaction methods in augmented reality training
items.abstract: Background As augmented reality (AR) adoption expands across training and operational domains, interaction design has served as a key determinant of user experience (UX). Although natural interaction techniques are believed to better support AR than traditional WIMP (windows, icons, menus, and pointing devices) interfaces, direct comparisons remain limited. Objectives This study compared natural and WIMP-based interaction paradigms in an individual, high-stakes procedural AR training task to evaluate their effects on usability, workload, presence, and task performance. Methods Thirty participants completed a within-subjects experiment using both interaction paradigms in a Tactical Combat Casualty Care AR training scenario delivered on a Meta Quest 3. Condition order was counterbalanced. Subjective outcomes included the System Usability Scale, NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), and Presence Questionnaire. Objective measures included task completion time, navigation errors, missed procedural steps, corrective actions, requests for clarification, and observed interaction smoothness. Paired-samples t -tests were used to compare conditions, with exploratory analyses examining order effects and relationships between immersive tendency and presence. Results Natural interaction produced significantly higher usability ( p = 0.009) and presence ( p = 0.001) than the WIMP interface. Participants also committed fewer navigation errors, missed fewer procedural steps, required fewer corrective actions, and demonstrated smoother interactions ( p < 0.05) in the natural condition. No significant differences were observed for workload, task completion time, clarification requests, or observed efficiency. An order effect indicated lower perceived workload during participants’ second session, regardless of interaction condition, suggesting a learning effect. Conclusion Natural interaction improves usability, presence, and interaction quality in individual, high-stakes procedural AR training while minimizing execution errors, although it does not necessarily improve speed or decrease cognitive workload during initial use. This evidence suggests that the principal benefits of natural interaction lie in improving the overall UX quality rather than maximizing efficiency, providing guidance for the design of future AR training systems.

items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) for Coding Open-Ended Survey Responses: A Total Survey Error Framework
items.abstract: Open-ended questions are commonly used in survey research to supplement closed-ended questions by capturing respondents’ views, reasons, and priorities in their own words. However, coding these responses for analysis remains time-consuming and difficult to standardise. Recent advances in automated coding, especially through large language models (LLMs), have renewed interest in using open-ended responses at scale, but their evaluation is often difficult and framed mainly in terms of classification accuracy and agreement with human coding. This paper develops a Total Survey Error framework for evaluating automated coding of open-ended survey responses as part of survey measurement and data production. Model outputs are assessed using existing human-coded data as a high-quality operational benchmark, with the evaluation examining six complementary dimensions, such as processing agreement, measurement validity, prevalence distortion, coding density, response-form sensitivity, and operational reliability. The framework is applied to data using open-ended survey responses from the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen). The paper aims to inform how automated coding systems, including LLMs, can be assessed in practice, and what issues survey researchers should consider when evaluating their suitability for open-ended survey coding, and how improved coding may enable wider use of open-ended questions in large-scale quantitative surveys. Keywords: automated coding; large language models; measurement validity; open-ended survey responses; survey data quality; Total Survey Error

items.title: Evaluating OpenEvidence Across Pediatric Subspecialties: A Guideline-Anchored Expert Review
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the quality, safety, and citation characteristics of OpenEvidence across pediatric subspecialties. METHODS: Guideline-anchored clinical questions spanning high, moderate, and low evidence certainty across 6 pediatric subspecialties were submitted to OpenEvidence. Expert reviewer pairs independently scored responses using the validated Quality Analysis of Medical Artificial Intelligence (QAMAI) instrument (6-30 range, higher scores indicate better quality) and a modified Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality harm assessment (0-7 range, higher scores indicate more harm), followed by consensus reconciliation. Citation analysis examined overlap with guideline references, claim substantiation, and pediatric specificity. Response consistency was assessed across 5 repeated queries. RESULTS: Seventeen questions were evaluated. The median QAMAI score was 27/30 (IQR, 24-29; "very good" quality). Potential harm was low (median 0/7, range 0-3), though 6 of 17 responses carried nonzero harm potential. OpenEvidence cited the primary guideline in 15 of 17 questions, yet only 17.6% of responses showed strong citation overlap (≥75% shared references) with the corresponding guidelines. OpenEvidence's citations reliably supported the claims they accompanied (88.2% with high substantiation), and 70.8% of reviewer assessments rated the evidence base as comparable in quality to that of the corresponding guidelines. In total, 35.3% of responses cited studies lacking pediatric specificity. Responses were clinically consistent across repeated queries (77.9% had no meaningful or only minor variation); no contradictory recommendations were observed. CONCLUSIONS: OpenEvidence produced high-quality responses with low expert-rated potential for harm across multiple pediatric subspecialties. The pediatric specificity of cited evidence warrants attention, reflecting the broader challenge of applying artificial intelligence tools that are trained on adult-predominant literature to pediatric populations.

items.title: Evaluation of the reliability, quality, and readability of multiple large language model responses (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) on silicosis
items.abstract: BackgroundInadequate or misleading health information about silicosis can delay diagnosis, reporting, and exposure removal, potentially affecting risk communication and timely occupational health interventions.ObjectiveThis study evaluates the reliability, quality, and readability of Large Language Models (LLMs) including ChatGPT (GPT-5), Gemini (2.5 Flash), and Copilot (Smart GPT-5), in answering patient-oriented silicosis questions, focusing on risk communication rather than clinical decisions.MethodsSilicosis-related questions were collected from online forums (September 1-7, 2025), and 25 frequently asked, clinically relevant questions were selected and submitted to the LLMs (September 8-14, 2025). Two occupational medicine specialists/pulmonologists independently evaluated responses (September 15-30, 2025) for reliability, quality, and readability using modified DISCERN, Global Quality Scale, and readability indices. Analyses used SPSS version 31.0.ResultsThe LLM-generated responses demonstrated fair reliability. Median (min-max) scores were 23 (12-27) for ChatGPT, 21.5 (14-29) for Gemini, and 26 (17.5-31) for Copilot. Copilot scored significantly higher than ChatGPT and Gemini (p = 0.014). GQS scores were similar across models (p = 0.102), with median scores of 4 (3-5) for ChatGPT and Copilot and 4 (2-5) for Gemini. Readability levels corresponded predominantly to secondary or tertiary education, with no significant differences between the models (all p > 0.05).ConclusionLLMs may enhance worker awareness but have limitations in accuracy and readability. They should complement, not replace, expert-supervised occupational health services. Future studies should align LLMs with international standards, improve accessibility, and establish governance frameworks for transparent and equitable AI use in occupational health.

items.title: Event Memory and Narrative Dynamics: A Large Language Model Framework for Multidimensional State Spaces
items.abstract: Studying event memory requires defining events and their relationships within remembered experience. Autobiographical narratives provide evidence of this organization, but their analytical units must first be established. This study introduces a large language model framework for constructing event representations from narratives and modeling their structure and dynamics with excerpt-level traceability. Explicit boundary rules and a feature schema informed by hippocampal models of episodic memory and navigation guide event construction. In a proof-of-concept application to interviews from five participants, the framework constructed 256 event-states. Multiple correspondence analysis embedded these states in feature-based spaces, with analyses focused on a selected 4-D geometry and 10-D and 13-D reference geometries. Consecutive event-states were significantly closer than expected under randomized narrative order. In the selected 4-D ten-basin solution, similarity between basin-state feature profiles corresponded with similarity between one-step routing profiles; context, mechanism, and theme differentiated full-system pathway engagement. A successor representation modeled expected basin-state occupancy across successive steps. Correlations between basin-centroid distances and complete successor-profile distances were positive across all five basin solutions, with exploratory tests supporting correspondence in at least two solutions across all three geometries. These findings connect feature-based event representations with observed narrative transitions and modeled multistep organization. The framework translates hippocampal principles into source-linked event boundaries and state representations, providing an analytical basis for testing neural accounts of event segmentation and predictive organization during naturalistic recall.

items.title: EventLens: Event-Structure Reinforcement Learning for Video Understanding
items.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong results on video question answering, yet often fail to recover the temporal structure that makes a video coherent. They may merge neighboring events, miss single-event progression, or infer implausible relations across events. We study structured temporal understanding as the ability to recover event structure from visual evidence, including event boundaries, single-event progression, and multi-event relations. We argue that this gap arises from a mismatch between current post-training objectives and temporal reasoning, where caption-style supervision allows models to rely on language shortcuts rather than visual temporal grounding. To address this, we propose EventLens, a vision-centric reinforcement learning framework that learns video understanding through event-structure recovery. Instead of reconstructing captions, EventLens trains models to recover temporal structure under controlled perturbations, such as altered temporal granularity, reversed progression, and shuffled event order. We instantiate this framework with a three-level temporal ontology and derive three verifiable task families: event segmentation, progression discrimination, and multi-event relation reasoning. These tasks admit deterministic rewards, enabling task-specialized GRPO training without human preference labels or learned reward models. We further introduce multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MT-OPD) to consolidate specialized policies into a unified model. Experiments on Qwen3-VL backbones show consistent improvements on temporal grounding and event-sensitive reasoning benchmarks, while preserving general video-QA performance. Learning curves further demonstrate that EventLens achieves comparable downstream transfer with significantly reduced training cost compared to direct mixed RL optimization.

items.title: Evidence-Centered Radiographic Grading of Knee Osteoarthritis: A Review of Deep Learning, Ordinal Modeling, Fusion, and Explainable AI
items.abstract: Automated severity grading of knee osteoarthritis (KOA) has progressed from handcrafted descriptors to deep networks, ordinal objective, attention mechanism and multimodal learning, and explainable artificial intelligence. The source presentation motivating this review focuses on fusion of complementary structur-al and textural radiographic evidence and hybrid learning and interpretable predic-tion. It is well supported recently in literature but some persistent problems can be noted: the classes are not equally sized, the separation of adjacent Kellgren–Lawrence (KL) grades are challenging, performance of the model can be below external validation, and the quality of the explanations is not measured quantita-tively. In this review, we categorize the methods used for grading KOA into handcrafted/radiomics, convolutional and transfer-learning systems, ordinal or hi-erarchical models, transformer and vision–language and fusion-oriented pipe-lines. According to comparative analysis, the contributions of architecture alone are hard to interpret, as there is a strong influence from composition of datasets, labeling practice, projection, preprocessing and validation design on reported measures. Evidence centered fusion is thus not a single network architecture, but a mixture of complementary representations, ordinally aware predictions, calibra-tion, and clinically grounded XAI. Priority directions for clinically credible de-ployment identified in the review include clinically relevant measures of uncer-tainty, quantitative assessment of the quality of explanations, imaging integrated with clinical or longitudinal evidence, leakage-safe splitting, and multi-center evaluation.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: Methods, Benefits, and Challenges for Trustworthy Clinical Decision Support
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly studied for tasks such as medical-image analysis, risk prediction, and clinical decision support. However, strong predictive performance does not by itself show why a model reached a particular conclusion or whether that conclusion is appropriate for a patient. This paper reviews explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods that can make healthcare predictions more understandable to clinicians and other stakeholders. A focused narrative review was conducted using foundational work on local explanations and Shapley-value-based feature attribution, a healthcare-focused review, and World Health Organization guidance on AI ethics. The paper compares model-specific and model-agnostic explanations, with particular attention to LIME, SHAP, and visual explanation methods. The review indicates that explanations can support error analysis, communication, and model auditing, but they should not be treated as proof that a prediction is correct, fair, or clinically safe. Explanation quality depends on data quality, model behaviour, the intended user, and the clinical context. The paper proposes a practical evaluation framework combining predictive performance, explanation fidelity, stability, clinical usefulness, fairness checks, and human oversight. It concludes that XAI should be integrated into the full lifecycle of clinical AI systems rather than added only after model development. Index Terms—Explainable AI, healthcare, clinical decision support, interpretability, SHAP, LIME.

items.title: Explainable Large Language Model for Intelligent Decision Support in Complex Domain
items.abstract: Despite showing great skills in working with unstructured data and generating appropriate answers, large language models (LLMs) cannot be applied in critical settings due to their lack of transparency and susceptibility to hallucination. The paper describes an approach to creating explainable LLM-based decision support systems, which includes breaking down complex questions into small subtasks that are processed via auditable pipelines. The approach employs retrieval-augmented generation along with domain-specific knowledge bases and computational instruments for the purpose of producing explanations and demonstrating intermediate reasoning steps while emphasizing data limitations. The approach is tested on clinical decision support problems for a multiple myeloma population. Comparing the results with those obtained when using monolithic LLMs as well as explainable machine learning approaches proves that structured decomposition leads to better decision traceability while achieving similar performance.
